title: Pine and cobalt deficiency in sheep
subtitle: Recognising and addressing cobalt deficiency, the cause of pine in young and adult sheep.
excerpt: Pine in sheep is the common name for cobalt deficiency, a condition that causes young lambs and adult sheep to waste, lose interest in food, and develop a characteristic watery eye discharge and pale skin. Cobalt is an essential mineral needed to synthesise vitamin B12 in the rumen. On cobalt-deficient soils, particularly upland acid soils, this deficiency is common and treatable but can kill if missed.

glossaryTerms.definition: The common UK name for cobalt deficiency in sheep. Affected animals waste and fade, giving the appearance of simply fading away (hence the name). Seen most often in lambs on cobalt-deficient upland and acid soils.

A shortage of the trace element cobalt, which rumen microbes need to synthesise vitamin B12. Without sufficient B12, sheep cannot efficiently metabolise propionate (a key energy pathway) and amino acids, leading to wasting.

A slow-release ruminal bolus that dissolves over three to twelve months in the rumen, supplying controlled amounts of trace elements including cobalt, selenium, and iodine. A practical approach to long-term trace element supplementation in sheep.

content.text: Cobalt is a trace element that rumen microbes use to produce vitamin B12 (cobalamin). Without enough cobalt in the diet, B12 production falls, and the sheep's energy metabolism and protein synthesis are impaired. The result is a wasting condition called
pine
: a slow, steady decline rather than an acute crisis.
Where it occurs

Pine is most common on upland, acid, or heavily leached soils in the UK: much of Wales, Scotland, the North Pennines, and parts of Dartmoor and Exmoor. Soil cobalt levels in these areas are often below the threshold needed to maintain adequate rumen B12 synthesis. Lowland grass leys rarely cause deficiency, but it can occur where lime and phosphate applications have reduced cobalt availability to the plant.
Signs
Gradual wasting and weight loss despite apparently adequate grazing.
Pale mucous membranes (gums, inner eyelid), a soft anaemia.
Watery eye discharge: a characteristic tear-staining on both sides of the face.
Reduced appetite and a general loss of interest in grazing. Affected lambs may stand separate from the group.
In severe cases: light sensitivity, blindness, and white liver disease.
Diagnosing cobalt deficiency
The signs above are not specific to cobalt: many conditions can cause wasting in lambs. A vet can confirm
cobalt deficiency

through blood samples (vitamin B12 levels) or liver tissue B12 at post-mortem of a casualty. Soil and herbage testing from your pasture gives a long-term picture of what trace element inputs the soil needs. Do not supplement with cobalt boluses or drench speculatively across the whole flock without a confirmed diagnosis: excess cobalt causes its own toxicity.
Treatment and prevention
Once cobalt deficiency is confirmed by a vet, the options are:
A
trace element bolus
containing cobalt, given annually at tupping or six to eight weeks before lambing. The bolus dissolves slowly in the rumen over months.
Cobalt-containing drenches given to lambs at specified intervals through the growing season. Effective but labour-intensive for large flocks.
Injectable vitamin B12 for a rapid response in deficient animals. Not a long-term fix, but appropriate while a prevention programme is set up.
Soil application of cobalt sulphate fertiliser, which increases cobalt uptake by the grass. Discuss with a vet or FACTS-qualified adviser before application.

Pine is sometimes confused with copper deficiency, which causes similar wasting but has different neurological signs (swayback in lambs, rather than the watery eye and general fading typical of pine). Copper toxicity is also a serious risk in sheep, who store copper readily and are sensitive to excess. Blood testing before supplementing is worth the effort.
